title: AQIU Decision — AQIU Adjudicatory Body decision re Mr Agron Zeqiri KOS
text:
DECISION OF THE
ADJUDICATORY BODY
As per Article 32.3 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code
Decision by:
Raymond Hack (South Africa), Chairperson
In the matter related to:
Mr. Agron Zeqiri (Kosovo), Respondent
Represented by Mr. Shkelzen Feka, Attorney-at-Law at Feka & Murati L.L.C,
Prishtina, Kosovo.
Regarding:
Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.6 and 9.9 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code
Lausanne, 28 May 2025
* * * * *

I. Overview
1. The present case relates to the conduct of the former President of the
Kosovo Swimming Federation (“KSF”), Mr. Agron Zeqiri (the “Respondent” or
“Mr. Zeqiri”).
2. More precisely, the Respondent was provisionally suspended on 12
September 2024 by the Chief Ethics and Compliance Officer (the “CECO”) of
the Aquatics Integrity Unit (“AQIU”) on the basis of various alleged acts of
misconduct. During his tenure as President of the KSF, the Respondent
allegedly abused his position and threatened and engaged in discriminatory
conduct towards two athletes, Mr. Adell Tsakhilov Sabovic (“Mr. Sabovic”) and
Ms. Hana Beiqi (“Ms. Beiqi”). This conduct included, inter alia, preventing their
participation in the 2024 World Aquatics Championships in Doha (“Doha
2024”) and attempting to prevent their participation in the 2024 Olympic
Games in Paris (“Paris 2024”).
II. Summary of Allegations
3. The following summary of the allegations made against the Respondent does
not purport to include every single contention put forth by the Parties during
these proceedings. However, the Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU has
thoroughly considered all evidence and arguments submitted, even if no
specific or detailed reference has been made to those arguments in the
following outline of its positions and in the ensuing discussion on the merits.
A. Discrimination and Threats against Mr. Sabovic
i. Doha 2024 World Aquatics Championships
4. On 9 December 2023, the KSF held a Board meeting to discuss Mr. Sabovic’s
request for membership in the KSF and his inclusion as a representative of
Kosovo in Doha 2024.
5. The Respondent participated in this meeting as a representative of the KSF,
as evidenced by the record of the Board meeting dated 9 December 2023,
and opposed Mr. Sabovic’s participation in Doha 2024.
6. This position was taken despite the fact that Mr. Sabovic was the highest-
ranked male athlete from Kosovo based on World Aquatics ranking points
(the “AQUA Points”) and the Respondent had confirmed to Mr. Sabovic in
writing that selection for competitions would be based on the AQUA Points.
Furthermore, Mr. Sabovic had already been formally authorised to represent
the KSF in aquatic competitions as of 1 January 2024, by an official letter from
the KSF Executive Board signed by the Respondent.
7. Nevertheless, Mr. Sabovic was informed that his exclusion was due to his non-
participation in the national championships, an event to which he was never
invited. Moreover, the KSF did not provide or attach to its decision any national
regulations or other selection criteria indicating that participation in the
national championships was a requirement to participate at Doha 2024.
8. Therefore, on 23 December 2023, Mr. Sabovic appealed the decision of the
KSF to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (“CAS”).

9. Following his appeal to the CAS, Mr. Sabovic received personal threats on 4
January 2024 from the Respondent, indicating that he would be suspended
or excluded from the KSF: “If a member of the KSF does not respect the
constitution might be suspended and not being a member of the KSF”.
10. On 28 March 2024, the CAS issued the award in which the Sole Arbitrator
ruled that it had no jurisdiction on the matter.
ii. Paris 2024 Olympic Games
11. As per the Paris 2024 Swimming Qualification, specifically the Universality
Places (Unqualified Athletes) (the “Universality Rules”), National Olympic
Committees (“NOCs”) that do not have athletes who have achieved an
Olympic Qualifying Time or an Olympic Consideration Time, as in the case of
Kosovo, could still enter a maximum of two (2) athletes, one male and one
female athlete, through Universality Places.
12. Pursuant to Article D.3 of the Universality Rules, there were four primary
criteria to enable one male and one female athlete to receive an invitation to
compete in Paris 2024:
i. Athlete must not be older than the age of thirty (30) years on January 1,
2024.
ii. Athlete must not have already participated in two prior Olympic Games.
iii. NOCs are obligated to enter the male athlete and the female athlete
who have achieved the highest AQUA Points table score in any
individual Olympic event, as achieved at a World Aquatics-approved
qualification event during the qualification period.
iv. Athlete must have competed in the World Aquatic Championships
2023 in Fukuoka (“Fukuoka 2023”) or in Doha 2024.
13. In April 2024, the World Aquatics Bureau abolished point iv of Article D.3 of
the Universality Rules.
14. On 24 June 2024, KSF informed World Aquatics that they had selected
athletes Mal Gashi (“Mr. Gashi”) and Ms. Beiqi to participate in Paris 2024. In
this context, World Aquatics was also informed that the highest-ranked
athletes, Mr. Sabovic was not selected as he allegedly did not meet the criteria
requirements for Paris 2024.
15. On 27 June 2024, the World Aquatics Executive Director, Mr. Brent J. Nowicki
(“Mr. Nowicki”) replied to KSF explaining that NOCs are obliged to enter the
athletes who have achieved the highest AQUA Points table score in any
individual Olympic event and that according to the Universality Rules, the
highest-ranked male athlete was Mr. Sabovic. In this context, it was also
explained that the deadline for a National Federation to request an exception
to World Aquatics for invitations based on Universality Places was 1 June
2024. Therefore, provided the KSF email of 24 June 2024 constituted a
request for exception, such request was late and could not be entertained.
The National Olympic Committee of Kosovo (“KOS NOC”) was copied to this
letter.

16. On 28 June 2024, the Respondent sent a letter to the KOS NOC, copying
World Aquatics. In that letter, the Respondent stated that Mr. Nowicki’s letter
conflicted with both local and international legislation and warned that any
attempts to implement Mr. Nowicki’s directives could have criminal
consequences.
17. Specifically, the Respondent claimed that Mr. Nowicki’s letter contained false
statements and expressed concern that World Aquatics had illegally
attempted in every possible way to send Mr. Sabovic to Paris 2024. The
Respondent further argued that Mr. Sabovic was not eligible to participate
because he had not competed in national competitions. Additionally, since he
acquired Kosovo citizenship through naturalisation, he would not meet the
criteria to participate in international competitions, including the Olympic
Games. To support this argument, the Respondent pointed out that Mr.
Sabovic had lost his case before the CAS.1 The Respondent also stated that if
the KOS NOC selected Mr. Sabovic for Paris 2024, the KSF would sue the KOS
NOC and request an injunction to halt the execution of this decision until the
court reached a final ruling.
18. On 4 July 2024, World Aquatics reiterated that, under the Universality Rules,
the highest-ranked athletes, based upon the AQUA Points were:
• Male – Adell SABOVIC
Men Freestyle 100m (Entry Time: 00:51.46)
• Female – Hana BEIQI
Women Freestyle 50m (Entry Time: 00:26.65)
19. On 5 July 2024, the Respondent called a press conferences to oppose Mr.
Sabovic’s participation in Paris 2024. In this context, remarks with reference
to the ethnicity of his parents were made by the Respondent calling Mr.
Sabovic “Serb” or “Russian”.
20. On 7 July 2024, Mr. Nowicki wrote to the Respondent to inform him that World
Aquatics had received an anonymous report concerning his comments on the
application of eligibility criteria outlined in the Universality Rules. The report
also indicated that a targeted campaign had been launched against Mr.
Sabovic, with “racist” language being used to criticise him.
21. In this context, the Respondent was informed that the report would be
forwarded to the AQIU. Additionally, he was reminded that Mr. Sabovic was
unequivocally the male athlete who had achieved the highest AQUA Points
table score in any individual Olympic event, as achieved at a World Aquatics-
approved qualification event during the Paris 2024 qualification period.
Despite having the opportunity to do so, neither the Respondent nor the KSF
timely appealed this determination or asserted any exceptional application of
the rules to World Aquatics or otherwise.
22. As a result, the KOS NOC entered Mr. Sabovic for Paris 2024.
B. Abuse of Power and Discrimination against Ms. Beiqi
23. Under the Universality Rules and as confirmed by Mr. Dale Neuburger, World
1 CAS 2024/A/10263, Adell Sabovic v. Kosovo Swimming Federation.

Aquatics Treasurer and Technical Delegate for Swimming, Ms. Beiqi was the
best female athlete from Kosovo based on AQUA Points relevant for Paris
2024.
24. However, in order to compete in Paris 2024, she was required to participate
in at least one of two World Aquatics Championships: Fukuoka 2023 or Doha
2024.
25. For Fukuoka 2023, the highest-ranked athletes based on AQUA Points
relevant for Paris 2024 were Mr. Gashi and Ms. Beiqi. However, the KSF
entered Mr. Gashi and the Respondent’s daughter, Ms. Eda Zeqiri (“Ms. Zeqiri”),
instead.
26. For Doha 2024, the highest-ranked athletes based on AQUA Points relevant
for Paris 2024 were Mr. Sabovic and Ms. Beiqi. Nevertheless, the KSF again
entered Mr. Gashi and Ms. Zeqiri, although this would prevent Mr. Sabovic and
Ms. Beiqi from being eligible for Paris 2024 and would give the Respondent’s
daughter a path to participate in Paris 2024.
27. On 2 February 2024, the KOS NOC, following a report from the Otrila Water
Sports Club, expressly requested the KSF to include Ms. Beiqi in Doha 2024.
The KSF disregarded this request.
28. As noted above, considering that Point IV was abolished in April 2024, Ms.
Beiqi was eligible to complete in Paris 2024.
III. Procedural Background
A. Preliminary Procedure before the CECO
29. On 16 July 2024, the AQIU notified the Respondent of the initiation of an
investigation and provided him with an opportunity to submit his position on
the matter. The Respondent did not respond to this letter.
B. Main Procedure before the CECO
30. On 12 September 2024, based on all information and documents received,
pursuant to Article 21 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code (the “Integrity
Code”), the CECO decided to impose a provisional suspension on the
Respondent given that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of
Aquatics was at risk.
31. At the same time, pursuant to Article 23 of the Integrity Code the CECO
decided to formally charge the Respondent by means of a notice of charge
(“Notice of Charge”) for possible violation of Article 7 of the World Aquatics
Constitution (the “Constitution”), Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.6 and Article 9.9 of the
Integrity Code:
i. Article 7 paragraphs b), c) and l) of the Constitution read as follows:
“Members are obliged:
[…]
b) to fully comply at all times with this Constitution and the World

Aquatics Rules, the WADA Code, the decisions and directives of the
World Aquatics Bodies, as well as the decisions of CAS;
c) to respect the principles of loyalty, integrity, sportsmanship and all
the values expressed in the Mission Statement of this Constitution;
[…]
l) to ensure that World Aquatics is not brought into disrepute in any way
whatsoever as a result of actions or omissions of the Member or of any
of its members, representatives, athletes, officials or any other person
subject to the Member.”
ii. Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3 and 5.6 - Duties of good conduct of the Integrity
Code read as follows:
“5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
5.3 Covered Persons must avoid acts or omissions that give the
appearance of impropriety, or that disparage World Aquatics, or that
bring (or have the potential to bring) World Aquatics, Aquatics and/or
sport generally into disrepute.
5.6 Covered Persons must avoid any act of discrimination against
anyone on the basis of race, skin colour, gender, religion, sexual
orientation, language, political or other opinion, national or social origin,
property, birth, disability or any other ground.”
iii. Article 9.9 - Duty of undivided loyalty of the Integrity Code reads:
“9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.”
32. According to the Notice of Charge, the CECO determined that a suspension
for a fixed period of four (4) years from taking part in any Aquatic-related
activities on behalf of World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or
World Aquatics Member and a fine of USD 25,000 should be the applicable
consequences in this case.
33. The Respondent was also informed that in accordance with Article 23.3 of the
Integrity Code, he may respond to the Notice of Charge in one of the following
ways:
i. admit the charge and accept the consequences and sanctions;
ii. admit the charge, but dispute and/or seek to mitigate all or any of the
potential consequences and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
consequences and sanctions; or
iii. deny the charge, and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the charge

and any consequences and sanctions.
34. On 19 September 2024, the Respondent denied the allegations against him
and requested the Adjudicatory Body to determine the charge and any
consequences and sanctions.
C. Procedure before the Adjudicatory Body
35. On 11 October 2024, the CECO referred the matter to the Adjudicatory Body.
36. On 14 October 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body, informed the
Respondent of his rights, including the opportunity to challenge the
composition of the single-member panel and to provide additional
information or written submissions.
37. On 17 October 2024, the Respondent requested an extension of his deadline
to provide a written submission and objected to the composition of the single-
member panel, requesting a three-member panel.
38. On 18 October 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body granted the
Respondent a one-week extension of the deadline but maintained his
position that a single-member panel is appropriate to adjudicate this matter.
39. On 28 October 2024, the Respondent provided his answer to the case referral
(the “Answer”).
40. On 11 November 2024, the Respondent informed the Chair of the Adjudicatory
Body that he was no longer represented by Mr. Fis Murati (“Mr. Murati”) but
was now represented by Mr. Shkelzen Feka.
41. On 13 November 2024, in light of this change in representation, the Chair of
the Adjudicatory Body granted the Respondent another opportunity to
submit any further written statements or supplementary documentation.
42. On 20 November 2024, the Respondent replied requesting that the
proceedings continue on the basis of the written submissions previously filed
by Mr. Murati.
43. On 17 December 2024, the Respondent requested an update on the case, in
particular regarding the validity of the provisional measures imposed on him,
as well as a request for a hearing.
44. On 19 December 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body confirmed that the
provisional suspension remains in force and will be duly considered in the
decision. Moreover, pursuant to Article 29 of the Integrity Code, the Chair of
the Adjudicatory Body considered itself sufficiently informed to render a
decision based on the written submissions. In coming to this conclusion, the
Chair of the Adjudicatory Body noted the fact that the Respondent was
afforded several opportunities to provide his position and that comprehensive
materials had already been provided. These materials include the 52-page
Answer, and the sixty-seven (67) exhibits submitted in support of the case.
45. On 2 April 2025, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body informed the Respondent
that the AQIU had been notified of a possible breach of the provisional
suspension imposed on him by the CECO on 12 September 2024, allegedly

occurring during the Skopje Open 2024 event during which the Respondent
would have been seen on the field of play. In light of the above, the
Respondent was granted an opportunity to provide his position.
46. On 21 April 2025, the Respondent replied, inter alia, that this allegation was
not supported by verified sources and official records from the event
organizers.
IV. CONSIDERATIONS OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
A. Jurisdiction, applicability of the Integrity Code and request for a hearing
47. In accordance with Article 17 of the Integrity Code, the AQIU is responsible for
adjudicating cases of potential violations of the Integrity Code.
48. Pursuant to Article 24 of the Integrity Code, the Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU
is responsible for adjudicating cases where a respondent has denied the
charges or requests laid by the CECO.
49. The above shows that the AQIU, and, more precisely, the Adjudicatory Body,
has jurisdiction over the case and is entitled to pass a decision on the basis of
the Integrity Code.
B. Burden and Standard of proof
50. The above having been established, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body
recalled that, as a general rule, the AQIU will have the burden of establishing
that an Integrity Code violation has been committed.
51. The standard of proof will be the balance of probabilities. Facts shall be
established by any reliable means. The Panel shall at its own discretion
determine the admissibility, relevance, materiality and weight of the evidence
offered.
52. The principle of strict liability applies. Therefore, violations are punishable
regardless of whether they have been committed intentionally, recklessly,
and/or negligently.
53. Having clarified the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body proceeded
to consider the merits of the case.
C. Merits of the case
i. Was the Respondent bound by the Integrity Code?
54. Since, at the time of the violations, the Respondent served as President of the
KSF, he falls within the definition of a “Covered Person” under Article 4.1 a) of
the Integrity Code namely: “persons who are, or are seeking to become
(whether by election or appointment or otherwise) World Aquatics Officials or
Other Officials.”
55. World Aquatics Officials is defined in the Integrity Code as: “Any person
elected or appointed to any position within World Aquatics, a Continental
Organisation or a World Aquatics Member, including but not limited to: - The
President, Vice-Presidents, Bureau members, Honorary Life Presidents,

Immediate Past President, Treasurer, and any candidates for election to the
Bureau […].”
ii. Did the Respondent violate Article 5.1 of the Integrity Code?
56. Articles 5.1, of the Integrity Code stipulate as follows:
“5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
57. After reviewing the full case file, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body considers
it has been established that the Respondent's failed to act honestly, fairly,
impartially and in accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity,
as he was required to do pursuant to Article 5.1 of the Integrity Code.
58. In this regard, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body observes that the
Respondent, in his capacity as President of the KSF at the time of the relevant
events, was under a heightened obligation to exemplify and uphold these
principles. However, he failed to meet these standards.
59. The Respondent deliberately excluded the highest-ranking athletes, namely
Mr. Sabovic and Ms. Beiqi, from participating in Doha 2024, fully aware that
such exclusion would effectively prevent them from qualifying for Paris 2024.
60. What is more, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that the non-selection
of Ms. Beiqi would have directly led to the selection of the Respondent’s
daughter, Ms. Zeqiri. In other words, by excluding Ms. Beiqi from Doha 2024,
the Respondent effectively created an opportunity for his own daughter to be
selected in Paris 2024 at her place.
61. Such conduct reflects a serious departure from the ethical standards required
under Article 5.1 of the Integrity Code and constitutes a misuse of authority
for personal gain, to the detriment of other athletes and the integrity of the
selection process.
62. In light of the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body deems that the
Respondent clearly violated Article 5.1 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code.
iii. Did the Respondent violate Article 5.2 of the Integrity Code?
63. Articles 5.2, of the Integrity Code stipulate as follows:
“5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with or
that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.”
64. The Objectives of the Integrity Code can be found in Articles 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 of
the Integrity Code:
“1.1 World Aquatics has adopted this Integrity Code to establish clear
integrity standards for persons involved in the activities of World Aquatics,
to protect the health, safety and well-being of Athletes, to prohibit conduct
that might undermine public confidence in the integrity of Aquatics and/or
in the uncertainty of outcome of Events, and to establish effective
mechanisms for enforcement of this Integrity Code and sanctions for any

violation.
1.2 World Aquatics is committed to uphold integrity in the governance and
administration of Aquatics as a basic principle of good governance and as
a fundamental precept of its autonomous role as the governing body of
Aquatics worldwide, in the best interests of the sport and its stakeholders.
1.3 World Aquatics is also committed to uphold the integrity of Aquatics on
the field of play. The essence of the Aquatics disciplines is the contest
between competing athletes and teams as an honest test of skill and ability,
the outcome of which is determined by (and only by) the contestants’
relative sporting merits. Any manipulation of sports competitions or other
conduct that might undermine public confidence in the integrity of the
sporting contest and/or in the uncertainty of its outcome is fundamentally
at odds with that essence of the Aquatics disciplines and must be
eradicated at all costs.”
65. Thus, Article 5.2 aims to prohibit conduct that might undermine public
confidence in the integrity of Aquatics, including decisions that are not made
in the in the best interests of the sport, its stakeholders, or the fundamental
principle of fair and transparent competition.
66. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body deems that the Respondent’s conduct
especially trying to favour his daughter over other athletes to go to the
Olympic Games, and threatening athletes, clearly had the potential to
undermine public confidence in the Integrity of Aquatics. In fact, such
behaviour compromises the principles of fairness and merit-based
competition and erodes trust in the Aquatics institutions as the public could
perceive that selection processes are influenced by personal interests or
coercion.
67. In light of the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body deems that the
Respondent clearly violated Article 5.2 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code.
iv. Did the Respondent violate Article 5.3 of the Integrity Code?
68. Article 5.3 of the Integrity Code stipulates as follows:
5.3 Covered Persons must avoid acts or omissions that give the
appearance of impropriety, or that disparage World Aquatics, or that bring
(or have the potential to bring) World Aquatics, Aquatics and/or sport
generally into disrepute.
69. In this respect, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body considers that the
Respondent’s actions, each for itself alone and taken together, give rise to a
strong and objective appearance of impropriety. For the Chair of the
Adjudicatory Body, there is no doubt that a president of a national Federation
threatening athletes and trying to favour his daughter to get her to the
Olympic Games gives an appearance of impropriety. Such conduct is
incompatible with the ethical standards expected of an individual holding a
position of influence within a sports federation, and is especially unacceptable
coming from the highest-ranking official in a National Federation—the
president—who is expected to exemplify integrity, impartiality, and leadership
at all times.
70. In light of the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body deems that the

Respondent clearly violated Article 5.3 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code.
v. Did the Respondent violate Article 5.6 of the Integrity Code?
71. Article 5.6 of the Integrity Code provides as follows:
"5.6 Covered Persons must avoid any act of discrimination against anyone
on the basis of race, skin colour, gender, religion, sexual orientation,
language, political or other opinion, national or social origin, property, birth,
disability or any other ground.”
72. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that, in the invitation letter for the
press conference held on 8 July 2024, the Respondent explicitly stated that
Mr. Sabovic’s participation in Paris 2024 constitutes a “sports scandal” and
that he would fight to prevent him from going to Paris. Moreover, as confirmed
by the report of a KSF Board Member and by media articles, the Respondent
allegedly orchestrated a targeted and slanderous campaign against Mr.
Sabovic, based on his origin, with explicit references to his Serbian or Russian
descent. The Respondent further argued that Mr. Sabovic could not represent
Kosovo as he was a naturalized citizen. Based on the above, the Chair
considers it established that the Respondent sought to prevent Mr. Sabovic
from representing Kosovo on the basis of his social origin.
73. By making discriminatory remarks towards Mr. Sabovic, the Respondent
engaged in conduct that is not only wholly unacceptable but also clearly in
violation of Article 5.6 of the Integrity Code which prohibits any form of
discrimination. The nature and tone of the Respondent’s remarks
demonstrate a clear breach of the duty to act with respect and dignity
towards all participants in the sport. Such conduct undermines the core
values of integrity and equality that the Integrity Code seeks to uphold.
74. In light of the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body finds that the
Respondent has clearly violated Article 5.6 of the World Aquatics Integrity
Code.
vi. Did the Respondent violate Article 9.9 of the Integrity Code?
75. Article 9.9 of the Integrity Code provides as follows:
"9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in any
way, especially for their own aims or objectives."
76. Lastly, by preventing Mr. Sabovic and Ms. Beiqi from participating in Doha
2024, by attempting to hinder their potential qualification and participation in
Paris 2024, and by simultaneously seeking to secure the participation of his
daughter, Ms. Zeqiri, in that same event, the Respondent acted in a manner
that constitutes a blatant conflict of interest and misuse of authority. These
actions are in direct breach of Article 9.9 of the Integrity Code, which prohibits
the use of one's position to influence decision-making processes for personal
gain or to the detriment of others. The Respondent’s conduct reveals a clear
pattern of partiality and self-interest, which not only compromises the rights
of the affected athletes but also calls into question the credibility of the
selection process and the integrity of the Respondent’s role. Such behaviour
gravely undermines the principle of merit-based competition, and the broader
trust placed in sporting bodies to act with neutrality and fairness.

77. In light of the foregoing, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body deems that the
Respondent clearly violated Article 9.9 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code.
vii. The Respondent claims he had no involvement with Mr. Sabovic’s
membership in the KSF
78. In his defence, the Respondent argues that he held no official position within
the KSF at the time of the Executive Board’s decision concerning Mr.
Sabovic’s membership in the KSF and his participation in Doha 2024. The
Chair of the Adjudicatory Body disagrees and considers this claim to be
inaccurate and contradicted by the evidence on record.
79. First and foremost, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that on 9
December 2023, the KSF held an emergency Board meeting to discuss Mr.
Sabovic’s request for membership in the KSF and his inclusion as a
representative of Kosovo at Doha 2024. The Respondent was present at this
meeting as a representative of the KSF and opposed Mr. Sabovic’s
participation in Doha 2024, as evidenced by the official Record of the Meeting.
This alone is sufficient to refute the Respondent’s position and demonstrates
not only his active engagement in KSF affairs at that time but also his direct
involvement in matters related to Mr. Sabovic’s membership.
80. Moreover, a letter signed by the Respondent on 23 December 2023 — the
same date on which he claims to have been elected President by the KSF
Assembly — explicitly authorised Mr. Sabovic to represent the KSF in aquatic
competitions as of 1 January 2024. The Respondent’s signature on this letter
further confirms his direct involvement in such matters.
81. Additionally, in response to a request from Mr. Sabovic seeking clarification on
the selection criteria for competitions, the Respondent confirmed in writing
that selection would be based on the number of AQUA Points. This further
highlights the Respondent’s active role in decision-making processes related
to athlete selection.
82. Furthermore, following Mr. Sabovic’s appeal to CAS against the decision
excluding him from participation in Doha 2024, the Respondent personally
threatened him on 4 January 2024. In a written message, the Respondent
stated: “If a member of the KSF does not respect the constitution, [he] might
be suspended and not [be] a member of the KSF.”
83. In light of the above, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body finds that the
Respondent was actively engaged in the affairs of the KSF and was
specifically involved in matters concerning Mr. Sabovic’s membership.
viii. The Respondent denies that Ms. Beiqi filed a complaint regarding her
exclusion from Doha 2024
84. The Respondent also claims that Ms. Beiqi did not submit any complaint or
request to KSF and that she expressed no dissatisfaction regarding her
exclusion from Doha 2024. Against this background, the Chair of the
Adjudicatory Body notes that, this is not accurate, nor is it a valid reason to
exclude the highest-ranked athlete from the competition. Ms. Beiqi’s
swimming club filed an official complaint with the KOS NOC after her exclusion
from Doha 2024, and the KOS NOC subsequently submitted a formal written
request to the Respondent for her inclusion in the competition, but this

request was blatantly ignored by the Respondent.
ix. The Respondent denies that Ms. Beiqi had higher points than Ms.
Zeqiri
85. Moreover, the Respondent supports that it is unfounded that Ms. Beiqi had
higher points than Ms. Zeqiri. However, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body
notes that in the letter sent by World Aquatics to KOS NOC, it was confirmed
that Ms. Beiqi was the highest-ranked female athlete based on AQUA Points
relevant for Paris 2024. This is further corroborated by the fact that at the end
Ms. Beiqi was the athlete nominated by the KSF to compete in Paris 2024.
x. The Respondent denies personal threats were made against Mr.
Sabovic
86. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body considers the assertion that no personal
threats were directed toward Mr. Sabovic to be incorrect. In the email dated 4
January 2024, sent by the Respondent to Mr. Sabovic, while the message
outlines the internal appeal procedures of the KSF in accordance with its
Constitution, the tone and context go beyond a mere informative
communication. The emphasis on the potential suspension for failure to
comply with the Constitution Act, as well as the risk of losing membership in
the KSF, clearly exerts pressure on Mr. Sabovic, who was seeking to defend
his rights through legal avenues before the CAS. Although the email
concludes with an expression of hoped-for cooperation, this does not negate
the fact that the overall message implies consequences for non-compliance,
reasonably perceived as a form of threat.
xi. The Respondent claims that Mr. Sabovic did not meet the procedural
and merits criteria
87. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that the decision to exclude Mr.
Sabovic from Doha 2024 on the basis that he “did not meet the procedural
and merits criteria” is directly contradicted by the Respondent’s own
statement dated 23 December 2023, as well as his prior communication to
Mr. Sabovic, in which he affirmed that selection for competitions would be
based on the number of AQUA Points.
xii. The Respondent claims that Mr. Sabovic was ineligible due to non-
participation in national competitions
88. Moreover, the justification that Mr. Sabovic was excluded due to his failure to
participate in national competitions (such as the 2024 Kosovo National
Championships) is without merit, as Mr. Sabovic was never invited nor
permitted to take part in those events. In the view of the Chair of the
Adjudicatory Body, this further demonstrates that the Respondent construed
artificial arguments with the intent of obstructing Mr. Sabovic’s opportunity to
compete in Doha 2024.
xiii. The Respondent claims that Mr. Sabovic was ineligible for Paris 2024
on the grounds of naturalized citizenship
89. As for the Respondent’s assertion that Mr. Sabovic was ineligible to compete
in international competitions, including the Olympic Games, due to his
naturalised citizenship, it is important to clarify that both World Aquatics and

the International Olympic Committee (“IOC”) apply strict eligibility procedures
in coordination with the relevant National Olympic Committees. At no point
have either the IOC or the KOS NOC raised any concerns regarding Mr.
Sabovic’s eligibility to compete in Paris 2024.
90. Mr. Sabovic was unequivocally the highest-ranked male athlete from Kosovo
based on the AQUA Points Table in an individual Olympic event, with the
relevant result obtained at a World Aquatics-approved qualification
competition during the applicable qualification period. Despite having the
opportunity to contest this determination, neither the Respondent nor the
KSF filed a timely appeal or raised any formal objection with World Aquatics.
As such, Mr. Sabovic’s nomination fully complied with the applicable
regulatory framework.
xiv. The Respondent claims Mr. Sabovic’s appointment for Paris 2024
violated domestic and international regulations
91. The Respondent’s claim that Mr. Sabovic’s appointment as Kosovo's
representative for Paris 2024 violated both domestic and international
regulations, and that World Aquatics officials infringed Article 3 of the
Constitution by abolishing Article D.3 of the Universality Rules to benefit Mr.
Sabovic, is without merit. In this respect, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body
notes that the Respondent failed to identify or substantiate any of the
domestic or international regulations allegedly breached, rendering these
claims unsubstantiated.
92. Moreover, in view of the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body, there was no violation
of Article 3 of the Constitution, which provides as follows:
“For the good of Aquatics and all Athletes, World Aquatics shall ensure that
all Aquatics are governed, organised, developed and managed in
accordance with the principles of democracy, right to equality, and no
discrimination between any race, skin colour, gender, religion, sexual
orientation, language, political or other opinion, national or social origin,
property, birth, disability or any other reason, neutrality, transparency,
accountability, fair play, inclusion, sportsmanship and clean sport. Above all,
Athletes are the central focus of World Aquatics' mission.”
93. To the contrary, the decision of the World Aquatics Bureau to abolish Article
D.3 of the Universality Rules was taken to safeguard the very principles
enshrined in Article 3 of the Constitution, which were blatantly violated by the
Respondent.
xv. The Respondent claims that Mr. Sabovic lost his case before the CAS
94. In addition, the Respondent’s claim that Mr. Sabovic lost case CAS
2024/A/10263, Adell Sabovic v. Kosovo Swimming Federation, is inaccurate
and misleading. In that matter, the CAS declined jurisdiction and did not rule
on the merits of the dispute. Accordingly, the Respondent’s reliance on the
outcome of case CAS 2024/A/10263 is misplaced and irrelevant to the
present case.
xvi. The Respondent denies having attempted to influence public opinion
against Mr. Sabovic
95. The Respondent’s denial of efforts to influence public opinion against Mr.

Sabovic is contradicted by the language of the Press Conference Invitation,
which refers to Mr. Sabovic’s inclusion on the KOS NOC list for Paris 2024 as
a “sports scandal” that “directly affects the state interests of the Republic of
Kosovo.” Such statements are inflammatory and serve to publicly undermine
Mr. Sabovic’s reputation and credibility. Furthermore, the invitation explicitly
asserts that Mr. Sabovic is not a legitimate representative of the KSF and
states that “NO ONE IS ABOVE THE LAW.” This language clearly seeks to
foster a hostile narrative against Mr. Sabovic and is inconsistent with the
Respondent’s claim of neutrality. It is evident that the Respondent’s actions
and rhetoric were capable of influencing public perception and fostering an
environment of hostility toward Mr. Sabovic.
xvii. Respondent claims that the allegations raised by the AQIU are
baseless
96. In response to the Respondent’s assertion that the allegations raised by the
AQIU are baseless, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that both the
Report of the KSF Board Member and a Media Article confirmed instances in
which the Respondent referred to Mr. Sabovic in a discriminatory manner,
specifically associating him with his Serbian or Russian origins. Such remarks
are unacceptable and reinforce the seriousness of the concerns raised.
xviii. The Respondent claims that Ms. Zeqiri and Mr. Gashi were
discriminated against in the selection for Paris 2024
97. The Respondent further alleges that athletes Ms. Zeqiri and Mr. Gashi were
discriminated against as a result of unlawful actions by certain officials of
World Aquatics and the KOS NOC, specifically by nominating Mr. Sabovic and
Ms. Beiqi for participation in Paris 2024, and by allegedly launching a
campaign against Ms. Zeqiri under the slogan “the President’s daughter.”
98. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body considers that this assertion is entirely
without merit and falls outside the scope of the present proceedings. As has
been extensively demonstrated above, the athletes who were subject to
discriminatory conduct in this matter are Mr. Sabovic and Ms. Beiqi, not Mr.
Gashi or Ms. Zeqiri. On the contrary, for the reasons detailed earlier, Mr.
Sabovic and Ms. Beiqi were the athletes with the highest number of AQUA
Points in their respective categories and were therefore entitled to participate
in Paris 2024. The Respondent, through his actions, attempted to prevent
these athletes from taking part in the competition, in clear contravention of
the applicable regulations. No campaign was ever launched using the phrase
“the President’s daughter.” Rather, it was merely recorded that the exclusion
of Ms. Beiqi from Doha 2024 must be regarded as intentional. Indeed,
considering that Ms. Beiqi had already been excluded from the World
Championships in Fukuoka 2023—prior to the subsequent abolition of point
(iv) of Article D.3 of the Universality Rules—such exclusion would have
rendered her ineligible for the Olympic Games in Paris 2024, effectively
leaving only the Respondent’s daughter, Ms. Zeqiri, as a viable candidate for
nomination.
xix. Did the Respondent violate Article 7 of the Constitution?
99. Article 7 paragraphs b), c) and l) of the Constitution stipulates as follows:
“Members are obliged:

[…]
b) to fully comply at all times with this Constitution and the World Aquatics
Rules, the WADA Code, the decisions and directives of the World Aquatics
Bodies, as well as the decisions of CAS;
c) to respect the principles of loyalty, integrity, sportsmanship and all the
values expressed in the Mission Statement of this Constitution;
[…]
l) to ensure that World Aquatics is not brought into disrepute in any way
whatsoever as a result of actions or omissions of the Member or of any of
its members, representatives, athletes, officials or any other person subject
to the Member.”
100. After review of the full case file, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body is not
satisfied that a violation of Article 7 of the Constitution was established
against the Respondent given that this Article applies to World Aquatics
Member Federations, as opposed to individual World Aquatics Officials.
D. Applicable sanction
101. As per Article 33.1 of the Integrity Code, the sanctions that can be imposed
for an Integrity Code Violation range from a reprimand to a lifetime
suspension.
102. Pursuant to Article 33.3 of the Integrity Code, aggravating factors that are
relevant to this case may include:
a) the age or experience or position of trust or authority of the Covered
Person;
[…]
c) any finding that the Covered Person violated more than one Article of this
Integrity Code or violated the same Article more than once;
[…]
e) any finding that the Covered Person’s violation affected or had the
potential to affect the course or outcome of an Event; […].
103. The Chair of the Adjudicatory Body acknowledges that the actions of the
Respondent were in clear violation of the Integrity Code, as well as the
principles of fairness and merit-based selection in sporting competitions.
Thus, it is essential to adopt a firm position toward any official who exploits
their role for personal benefit.
104. In the present case, the Respondent's behaviour represents a serious abuse
of his position, aimed at improperly influencing the selection process to
secure his daughter’s participation in Paris 2024. Such conduct
compromises the integrity and spirit of the sport and contravenes the
principles of fairness and equal opportunity that govern the Olympic selection

process. It reflects a clear conflict of interest and a misuse of authority, which
cannot be tolerated in any context.
105. Moreover, the Respondent’s actions involved discriminatory behaviour and
included attempts to intimidate athletes and obstruct their right to seek legal
redress. This type of conduct is entirely unacceptable and must be
unequivocally denounced, as it not only affects the athletes directly involved
but also erodes the credibility and legitimacy of sport governance. The AQIU
bears the fundamental responsibility to safeguard athletes’ rights and to
ensure that officials who abuse their authority are held to account.
106. It is equally essential that all World Aquatics Officials refrain from any conduct
that could undermine or brings World Aquatics into disrepute. Officials are
stewards of the sport’s values and must lead by example to preserve its
integrity and public trust.
107. In view of the above, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body concurs with the need
to impose a firm sanction. This measure is not only warranted in light of the
Respondent’s conduct but is also vital to serve as a deterrent against future
misconduct of a similar nature. Upholding the credibility of the Aquatic sport
requires clear and consistent consequences for breaches of the Integrity
Code at the highest level.
108. Accordingly, after careful consideration of the entire case file and the
arguments presented by the Respondent, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body
hereby determines that the following disciplinary measures constitute an
appropriate, proportional and just sanction for the Respondent:
a) a four-year period of ineligibility from holding any position within World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics
Member, including acting as President of the KSF. The suspension
imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent him from taking part in
any aquatic-related activities and/or events on behalf of World Aquatics,
any World Aquatics Continental Organisation, or any World Aquatics
Member Federation or recognised body, as well as participating or
attending, in any capacity, in any aquatic competition; and
b) a fine of USD 25,000. Failure to pay the fine shall prevent the
Respondent from holding any position within World Aquatics, any World
Aquatics Continental Organisation, or any World Aquatics Member
Federation or recognised body as well as from taking part in any aquatic-
related activities and/or events on behalf of World Aquatics, any World
Aquatics Continental Organisation, or any World Aquatics Member
Federation or recognised body, and participating or attending, in any
capacity, in any aquatic competition, until payment is made.
E. Start Date of the Period of Ineligibility
109. The period of Ineligibility shall, in principle, commence on the date of issuance
of the present decision.
110. That said, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body notes that the Respondent was
provisionally suspended by the CECO as of 12 September 2024.
111. With regard to the alleged breach of the provisional suspension by the

Respondent, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body observes that, at this stage,
there is insufficient evidence to conclude that a violation has in fact occurred.
However, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body reserves the right to review this
position should additional information come to light.
112. In light of the above, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body considers that the
time served under the provisional suspension must be credited against the
suspension impose.
113. Thus, the sanction shall begin on the day the Respondent was provisionally
suspended, i.e. 12 September 2024.

V. DECISION OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
(i) The AQIU has jurisdiction over this matter.
(ii) The Respondent has violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.6 and 9.9 of the
World Aquatics Integrity Code.
(iii) The Respondent is sanctioned with:
a. A four-year period of ineligibility from holding any position within
World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World
Aquatics Member, including acting as President of the KSF. The
suspension imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent him
from taking part in any aquatic-related activities and/or events
on behalf of World Aquatics, any World Aquatics Continental
Organisation, or any World Aquatics Member Federation or
recognised body, as well as participating or attending, in any
capacity, in any aquatic competition. The sanction begins on the
day the Respondent was provisionally suspended, i.e. 12
September 2024.
b. A fine of USD 25,000. Failure to pay the fine shall prevent the
Respondent from holding any position within World Aquatics,
any World Aquatics Continental Organisation, or any World
Aquatics Member Federation or recognised body as well as from
taking part in any aquatic-related activities and/or events on
behalf of World Aquatics, any World Aquatics Continental
Organisation, or any World Aquatics Member Federation or
recognised body, and participating or attending, in any capacity,
in any aquatic competition, until payment is made.
(iv) This decision is rendered without costs and will be made public.
(v) As per Article 35 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code, this decision
can be appealed to CAS within twenty-one (21) calendar days of the
appealing Party’s receipt of the written reasoned decision in
question by email.
